## Timings and citations

- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.

## POSITIONS and FACTS

POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.

Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".

## The gap ledger

The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).

A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.

- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.

Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.

A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.

The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.

## Reading the record

Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:

    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh

- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.

A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.

Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:

    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE

## Writing to the record

- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
  - what it means for the work;
  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.

Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.

    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"

To add a row:

1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.

To change a row:

- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. It refuses a note that takes the row past 1,200 characters, or its notes cell past 700 characters. `$L note N TEXT --check` writes nothing. It says whether TEXT fits, and how many characters the notes and the row have left now and would have left with TEXT. These counts include the separator that the tool adds. It exits 0 if TEXT fits, and 1 if not. Run it before a long note, or before a note on a row near its limits. If TEXT does not fit, shorten it, or cut the notes with `rewrite` (below).
- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.

- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.

## 1. Coherence

The design is one rule: a numeral converts where it stands, into the declared type, else into the machine default. Six cases get two answers or none; each has a repair.

Repair: a place fixes a type when its declared type declares a coercion from the numeral type (the eight number types; a program's type by point 4) or is a numeral type; every other type, and no type, takes the default. Then `f(3)` at `Number` is a `ZZ32`, and a tuple at `Any` defaults element by element.
- Two answers: "by its value" where the value is unknown. Row 946 shows it: a variable of numeral type reads `ZZ32` whatever its value. Inside `coerce(x: RadixPointNumeral)`, `t = x` is such an expression; so is a `nat` used as a value, whose value a template does not know (probe §8). Repair: the default applies to a numeral, a literal after the fold, never to an expression of numeral type; a `nat` used as a value has the type the Draft gives, `NN32` (`trait-parameters.tex:84-86`), or `ZZ32` (P-40), chosen once.
- Two answers: the fold against the fields. Point 4 reads the written numeral's four numbers; point 5 folds `7/2`, `-3` and `0.1 + 0.2` into "one numeral", which has no written form: the prototype made `1/3` a radix-3 numeral (probe §1, step 3), and a negative result has no `nat v`. Repair: the fold yields a constant with a sign, as the Draft's `IntegerConstant[\false, 3+5\]` has one (`constant.tex:49-52`): an integer constant defaults as an integer numeral, a quotient to `QQ`, one with a radix point to `RR64`; a program's coercion sees the four numbers of a written numeral only.
- Two answers: a static argument that several numerals fix. `<|3000000000, 0.5|>` is a `List[\RR64\]` if each numeral converts exactly into one instantiation, refused if each defaults first (`ZZ64` into `RR64` is written, P-74); an `if` join likewise. Repair: the narrowest default holding every value, `RR64` where any has a radix point, each converting into it exactly: the tie rule's form (`inference.tex:313-317`).
- Two answers: a program's type with no coercion from the numeral type. The prototype chained default and own coercion (probe §10, decision 3); the Draft says coercion does not chain (`conversions-coercions.tex:407-408`). Repair: refuse, or name the chain as the one exception.
- Undefined: "once per class, at load" as a semantics. For a reference object two evaluations of `c: CC64 = 3` become one object, which `SEQV` sees (`objects.tex:51-53`), and a raising coercion fails at load. Repair: a numeral at a program's type denotes one object, as a string literal does (P-171), or hoist value types only.

- P-173 **A numeral converts where it stands: where its place fixes a type, into that type at compile time from its exact value; where nothing fixes one, into the machine default, a `ZZ32`, or a `ZZ64` or `ZZ` when its value does not fit, and with a radix point an `RR64`.** A place fixes a type when its declared type has a coercion from the numeral type, as the eight number types have and a program's own type may (P-174), or is a numeral type; `Any`, `Object`, `Number`, an unbounded type parameter and no declared type take the default. So `x = 3` is a `ZZ32`, and `x SEQV z` is `true` for `z: ZZ32 = 3`; `bigN = 3000000000` is a `ZZ64` at its binding (row 946). The default applies to a numeral, a literal after the fold, never to an expression of a numeral type, and a `nat` parameter used as a value is a `ZZ32` (P-40). A type parameter that several numerals fix takes the narrowest default that holds every value, an `RR64` where any has a radix point, each numeral converting into it exactly; a float numeral whose conversions into `QQ` and `RR64` tie reads `RR64`. At a typed place the conversion is exact or rounds once (P-76, P-172), and a numeral outside the type's range is refused statically; walk converts from the exact value at the same places, place by place, before it runs the checker (P-12). An expression of numerals alone folds exactly before the checker into a signed constant, which defaults as an integer numeral, as a `QQ` for a quotient, or as an `RR64` with a radix point: so `x = 7/2` is a `QQ`, `1/2 = 0.5` is `true` through `QQ`'s `=` pair, and `-2147483648`, prefix minus on a numeral, folded, is a `ZZ32`. The library's `=` pairs over the numeral types stay, their conversion of a numeral folded. `gg(5, w)`, with `gg` declared at `(ZZ32, T)` and at `(Any, Any)`, runs the `ZZ32` declaration (P-49). Why: the design completes the Working Draft's, whose numerals have types of their own so that a library decides by coercions how they meet other types (P-174 gives that ground). It bends P-26 in two places, the numeral types' names and the places that fix no type, where the compiler's prelude, the team's later word, keeps the numeral's own type; the curator takes the bend by his right to finish the specification. He declined exact defaults, `ZZ` and `QQ` (the 2012 restart gives `NN` and `QQ`, `literals.tick:25`), since microGPT's untyped hyperparameters (`MicroGptFlat.fss:18`) would then be rationals and every untyped index would need `asZZ32`. The Draft's text that it contradicts, for Appendix I: numerals "not directly converted" and "polymorphic" (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:132-141`) at places that fix no type, and a `nat` parameter usable wherever an `NN32` variable is (`basic/trait-parameters.tex:84-86`); P-174 names the binary chapter's. What it keeps and changes in form: the judgement's section 3. Detail: `reviews/literal-design-judgement-2026-11-08.md`, sections 1 to 6 and the 42 test programs of its appendix; the prototype, `compile-ladder/plan-29/probes/literal-default.md`.

- P-168 **What `SEQV` means, on both paths: the specification's rule, with no special case for any type but the numeral types.** Values of different types are never strictly equivalent; two value objects of one type are when their fields are, tuples element by element and floats by their bit patterns; two reference objects are only when they are one object (`Specification/basic/objects.tex`, "Object Equivalence" and "Value Objects"). The one exception: two values of a numeral type inside a coercion's body are strictly equivalent when their reduced values are equal, so `2.5` and `2.50` are there (P-174). Both paths read the `value` modifier. Each path changes its own code: walk drops its equivalence across types (row 909) and its answer `true` for value objects whose body declares no field (row 113); the compiled helper `equality.sEquiv` gains the rule for value objects, tuples and floats (rows 906 and 907; the prelude's own `===` keeps row 908 until the switch-over). `ZZ`'s and `QQ`'s values are value objects (P-166). Strings are reference objects: the library declares `FlatString`, `CatString` and `SubString` without `value`, so two such strings are strictly equivalent only when they are one object, and text equality is the strings' own `=`; P-171 makes two literals of one text one object. This overrules the team's code on both paths, walk's `seqv` and the prelude's `opr ===(a:String, b:String) = a=b`, where the specification is silent on strings. A program with a `value object CC64` tests it on both paths beside the review's 14 cases (F-326). Why: the specification's rule read as written, over the team's unfinished code of 2008 and 2010, which its authors called preliminary and incomplete; P-167 makes this one comparison that both paths answer. Detail: `reviews/any-carrier-2026-11-06.md`, section 2.4; `reviews/string-equivalence-2026-11-06.md`, sections 3 and 7.

### Step 1, the library: `FloatLiteral` apart, its coercions, the float tie rule, the literal `=` pairs dropped

- `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fsi` and `.fss`: `value object FloatLiteral extends RR64` becomes `value object FloatLiteral extends Number`, which declares its own `asFloat(self): Float` (P-165). It stays an object, not the prelude's trait: walk makes `FFloatLiteral` values through its native constructor `interpreter/glue/prim/FloatLiteral.java` and calls its three glue bindings (section 4.5). An object excludes every type it does not extend, so `excludes { RR32, RR64 }` holds without the clause.
- `RR64` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi`, `.fss`): `comprises { Float }`, and `coerce(x: FloatLiteral) = asFloat(x)`, one rounding (walk's `FFloatLiteral.getFloat` is `Double.valueOf` of the text).
- `QQ`: `coerce(x: FloatLiteral) = numeralRatio(x.asString)`, exact: a new private function of 14 lines reads the decimal text into `n / d`.
- `RR32`: `coerce(x: FloatLiteral) = narrow(asFloat(x))`. Under walk this rounds twice; the compiled path folds it with one rounding (step 3). One rounding under walk needs a float parse of the text, which no helper has (`nativeHelpers` has `simpleDoubleArith.parseDouble` only).
- The `=` pairs over the literal types dropped, 15 in each of the api and the component: `RR64`'s, `QQ`'s, `ZZ32`'s, `ZZ64`'s, `NN64`'s, `ZZ`'s and `NN32`'s `opr =(self, b: IntLiteral)`, and `IntLiteral`'s own eight. No `=` pair over `FloatLiteral` was added.
- The float tie rule, in the checker (`impls/Functionals.scala`, `isNumeral` and `numeralReading`): a numeral with a radix point counts as a numeral at a tie and reads as `RR64`. I put it in step 1 because the library change alone makes ties (step 1a below).
- `Float`'s `asFloat(self)` returns `RR64` instead of `Float` (`FortressBuiltin.fss:82`): with `RR64` comprising `Float` alone the checker reads the two domains as equal and asks each return type to fit the other (step 1b below).

- problem: walk keeps a float numeral at `RR64` a `FloatLiteral` (row 943, `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md:635`), `QQ` takes no float numeral (row 944, `:636`), `NN32`, `NN64` and `RR32` refuse numerals (row 454, `:610`), `RR64` refuses 3000000000 (row 443, `:609`), `u + 1` at `NN32` is a `ZZ64` (row 484, `:156`), `round(2.5_10)` throws (row 361, `:602`), and `IntLiteral`'s own arithmetic answers a `ZZ32` (row 578, `:620`)
- spec: `Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:132-148` (numerals have their own types, which libraries convert by coercions) and `:83-129` (the four numbers); `Specification/basic/expressions/literals.tex:145-153`
- precedent: `value object Ratio(num: ZZ, den: ZZ) extends { QQ }` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:648` at the base), the prototype's library step (`explorations/compile-ladder/plan-29/probes/literal-default.patch:1-400`), and `Types.CHARACTER`'s switch by library (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/Types.java:78-91` at the base)
- deviation: walk converts a numeral into the eight number types through the library's own coercion, called once per site and type, not by a Java conversion per type (fork N7) (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/Coercions.java:88-115`); `RR32`'s rounding binding sits in `FortressBuiltin`, beside `RR32`, and `RR64`'s and the numerals' in `FortressLibrary` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss:208-210`, `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:668-670`); `strToFloat` gains a `ZZ32` base, a line beyond the declarations the brief names (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4839-4840`)
- historical: `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi`, `Library/FortressLibrary.fss`, `Library/Constants.fsi`, `Library/Constants.fss`, `Library/ReflectiveQuickCheck.fss`, `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fsi`, `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss`, `compiler/Types.java`, `scala_src/typechecker/impls/Functionals.scala`, `nativeHelpers/simpleDoubleArith.java`, `interpreter/env/LazilyEvaluatedCell.java`, `interpreter/evaluator/{BaseEnv,Evaluator,EvaluatorBase,Init,LHSEvaluator}.java`, `interpreter/evaluator/values/{FBigNum,FFloat,FInt,FLong,FOrdinaryObject,FunctionClosure,GenericFunctionOrConstructor,MethodClosure,NonPrimitive,OverloadedFunction,OverloadedMethod}.java` (under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/`), and the team's tests `ProjectFortress/tests/NumberPrintTest.fss`, `sequivTest.fss`, `XXXextendIntLiteral.fss`, `XXXextendFloatLiteral.fss`

Every stage and suite named below ran on the commit it names.

## What changed and why

**The library.** `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:454-494` and `.fss:668-721` declare, beside `Ratio`, `trait Numeral extends Number comprises { NaturalNumeral, RadixPointNumeral }` with the four getters abstract (`digits`, `fractionDigits` and `radix` at `ZZ32`, `digitValue` at `ZZ`), and the value objects `NaturalNumeral(digits: ZZ32, radix: ZZ32, digitValue: ZZ)`, whose `fractionDigits` is 0, and `RadixPointNumeral(digits: ZZ32, fractionDigits: ZZ32, radix: ZZ32, digitValue: ZZ)`. Each has `asString`, the numeral as the Working Draft writes one (its digits in its radix, at least `digits` of them, upper case, the radix point after `digits - fractionDigits` of them, `_r` where the radix is not ten), `asFloat(self): RR64` by one rounding, and its reversed `=` pairs: `NaturalNumeral` at the eight number types, `RadixPointNumeral` at `RR64`, `QQ` and `RR32`, each `do c: T = self; (c = b) end` as the library writes its pairs (`.fss:418` at the base). The number types' coercions, renamed or new, each with its pair:

| type | coercions from the numeral types, and their bodies | pair |
|---|---|---|
| `RR64` | `coerce(x: NaturalNumeral) = asFloat(x)`, `coerce(x: RadixPointNumeral) = asFloat(x)` (`.fss:389-390`) | both (`.fss:419-420`) |
| `QQ` | `Ratio(x.digitValue, 1)`; `x.digitValue / r^(x.fractionDigits)` for `r: ZZ = big(x.radix)`, reduced by `ZZ`'s `/` (`.fss:565-569`) | both (`.fss:588-589`) |
| `AnyIntegral` | `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` or `ZZ` by the value, which is never negative (`.fss:723-728`) | none, as at the base |
| `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN64`, `ZZ` | `x.digitValue.asZZ32`, `.asZZ64`, `.asNN64`, `x.digitValue` (`.fss:829`, `:935`, `:1045`, `:1155`) | `NaturalNumeral` (`:845`, `:956`, `:1064`, `:1175`) |
| `NN32` | `x.digitValue.asNN32` (`FortressBuiltin.fss:430`) | `NaturalNumeral` (`:453`) |
| `RR32` | `numeralRR32(x.digitValue, x.radix, 0)` and `numeralRR32(x.digitValue, x.radix, x.fractionDigits)` (`FortressBuiltin.fss:214-215`) | both, new (`:258-259`) |

`RR64` comprises `{ Float }` (`.fsi:294`); `Float`'s `asFloat(self): RR64` (`FortressBuiltin.fss:82`); the `^` over the numeral in `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN64`, `ZZ` and `NN32` renamed, its body `self^(b.digitValue.asZZ32)`; `pi` and `e` at `RR64` (`Library/Constants.fsi:16-17`, `.fss:15-16`); `ReflectiveQuickCheck.fss:40` chooses `theType[\ZZ32\]()` where it chose `IntLiteral`, and the arm `theType[\IntLiteral\]() => Just[\AnyGen\](genZZ32)` (`:157` at the base), which repeated the `ZZ32` arm above it, is dropped. `value object IntLiteral` and `value object FloatLiteral` leave `FortressBuiltin.fsi` and `.fss` with their 24 glue bindings; no line of the one library names either now. The glue classes `interpreter/glue/prim/IntLiteral.java` and `FloatLiteral.java`, and walk's `FIntLiteral` and `FFloatLiteral`, stay in the tree, unused (fork N11).

**The helper pair** (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/nativeHelpers/simpleDoubleArith.java:264-307`): `public static double numeralToDouble(BigInteger v, int r, int m)` and `public static float numeralToFloat(BigInteger v, int r, int m)`, the value `v / r^m` rounded once to the nearest double or float, ties to even, subnormals included, by an integer quotient at the format's last significand bit and its remainder; two private helpers (`lsbExponent`, `roundedQuotient`) whose types all map to Fortress, as the wrapper generator needs. The bindings: `private numeralRR64(v: ZZ, r: ZZ32, m: ZZ32): RR64` in `FortressLibrary.fss:668-670`, which both numerals' `asFloat` call, and `private numeralRR32(v: ZZ, r: ZZ32, m: ZZ32): RR32` in `FortressBuiltin.fss:208-210`, which `RR32`'s coercions call; walk carries `ZZ` in `BigInteger`, `ZZ32` in `int`, `RR64` in `double` and `RR32` in `float` (F-299). Walk's default for a radix-point numeral calls `numeralToDouble` in Java (`Numerals.java`), so the default and `RR64`'s coercion round alike.

**Walk's numerals** (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/Numerals.java`, new). `Evaluator.forIntLiteralExpr` and `forFloatLiteralExpr` (`Evaluator.java:1632`, `:1636`) return the value of the numeral's site, made once: its default, a subclass of `FInt`, `FLong`, `FBigNum` or `FFloat` (their constructors opened to the package) that carries a `Site` with the four numbers. The digits as written come from the numeral's text, since the node keeps the value and not the trailing zeros (`3.14150` has `digitValue` 314150, `fractionDigits` 5). The places:

- a typed binding, a field and an assignment (`LHSEvaluator.java:115`, `:220-230`, `BaseEnv.java:332`, `LazilyEvaluatedCell.java:69`), a parameter (`NonPrimitive.java:247`, `:272`), and a declared return type (`FunctionClosure.java:212-221`, `MethodClosure.java:85-89`, `Numerals.atReturn`): where the default does not fit the type, `Coercions.coerce` makes a numeral the numeral object at a numeral type, else converts it through the place type's coercion whose parameter type is the narrowest holding the numeral type, with no chain through the default (`Coercions.java:59`, `:88-115`, `:268`); the result is kept for the site and type (`Numerals.converted`), so a site gives one object of a reference type; a store keeps the default alone (`Numerals.plain`, deep for tuples);
- an integer numeral outside an integer type's range is not converted, so the place refuses it as walk refused one at a binding before: 'Type mismatch binding 3000000000' (`Numerals.inRange`);
- dispatch (`OverloadedFunction.java:2278-2342`, `:2712`): a declaration fits a numeral as it is where its parameter is the numeral's own type or admits its default; of those, the one that the defaults alone fit, unless the own-type fit's domain lies strictly below it; with no fit, the coercion attempt, each numeral converting only from its own type; and a tie among those, an ambiguous coercion, reads each numeral at its default; a functional method chosen at a numeral's own type receives the numeral object before walk finds the method on it (`Coercions.withNumeralObjects`). The three dispatch caches key a numeral apart from a value of its default type (`Numerals.keys`; `OverloadedFunction.java:99`, `OverloadedMethod.java:29`, `GenericFunctionOrConstructor.java:24`);
- the head of `EvaluatorBase.inferAndInstantiateGenericFunction` (`EvaluatorBase.java:90`): the inference reads each numeral at its default, and where the numerals at one type parameter's positions include a radix point, one beyond `ZZ32` by a `ZZ32` stand-in, so that walk's promotion gives `RR64`; the call's numerals then convert at the instance;
- `SEQV` (`FOrdinaryObject.java:48-49`): two numeral objects compare by `digitValue / radix^fractionDigits`, reduced, across both numeral types;
- `Init.java:46` empties the sites between runs.

**The checker.** `Types.INT_LITERAL` and `FLOAT_LITERAL` are no longer final and switch with the libraries, as `CHARACTER` does: the prelude's `IntLiteral` and `FloatLiteral` under the compiler's, `FortressLibrary`'s `NaturalNumeral` and `RadixPointNumeral` under the one library (`Types.java:61-62`, `:75-95`). `Functionals.isNumeral` counts a numeral with a radix point, and `numeralReading` reads one as `RR64` (`Functionals.scala:418-444`), the prototype's tie rule, written inside the two functions and with no new function, since rung C adds functions near them.

## For FACTS

**Walk's numeral is its default, carrying the numeral's four numbers, and converts from them where its place fixes a type.** An integer numeral is a `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` or `ZZ` by its value, a radix-point numeral the `RR64` nearest its value, one value per site (`interpreter/evaluator/values/Numerals.java`); at a typed binding, an assignment, a field, a parameter, a declared return type and a coercion it converts through the place type's coercion from `NaturalNumeral` or `RadixPointNumeral`, called with the numeral object, one result per site and type, and a store keeps its default alone; dispatch fits it as it is at its own type or its default, then by its own type's coercions only, and reads a tie at the default. What it means: F-74's walk half by value stands where nothing fixes a type, and walk answers a typed place as the checker does; a program's own type receives a numeral only through its coercion from a numeral type. ## Revival change

**The change.** The team's library gave a numeral the interpreter's own objects: `value object IntLiteral extends { Number }` with 21 glue bindings and `value object FloatLiteral extends RR64` with 3 (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fsi:199-246`, `:44` at the base), and the team's walk evaluated an integer numeral to a `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` or `ZZ` value by its value and a radix-point numeral to a `FloatLiteral` holding its text (`interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java:1631-1637` and `values/FFloatLiteral.java:21-33` at the base), so a float numeral stayed a `FloatLiteral` at an `RR64` binding and no number type but `RR64` received it.
